questions.q: Fill up: The fenestration slits of the capillary endothelium with fenestrations are ______ in diameter.
questions.exp: Fenestration slits: 50–100 nm diameter (30–50 nm belongs to the podocyte filtration slits). (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: The endothelial fenestrations are coated with ______, whose negative charge repels negatively charged proteins.
questions.exp: Coated with podocalyxin → −ve charge repels negatively charged proteins; heparan sulfate proteoglycans belong to the GBM. (Book p730)

questions.q: The function of the fenestrated capillary endothelium is to prevent proteinuria (albuminuria) and thereby prevent:
questions.exp: Function: prevent proteinuria (albuminuria) → prevent nephrotoxicity. (Book p730)

questions.q: PSGN, the disease of the capillary endothelium, stands for:
questions.exp: PSGN = Post Streptococcal Glomerulo Nephritis (printed as three words), the disease of the capillary endothelium. (Book p730)

questions.q: All of the following are described with the capillary-endothelium disease PSGN EXCEPT:
opts: Exudative neutrophilic infiltration of the lumen
questions.exp: PSGN (capillary endothelium disease): microhematuria, minimal proteinuria, exudative neutrophilic infiltration of lumen — not nephrotic-range proteinuria. (Book p730)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about PSGN as an endothelial disease is TRUE?
opts: It carries no risk for CKD
It carries a high risk of progression to CKD
questions.exp: The PSGN sub-bullet prints 'No risk for CKD.' — an absolute source claim taught as printed (with microhematuria, minimal proteinuria and exudative neutrophilic infiltration). (Book p730)

questions.q: Which sequence matches the book's pathophysiology of CKD chain?
opts: ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons → intraglomerular HTN → capillary stretching → ↑ pore diameter → proteinuria
Hyperfiltration → ↓ functional nephrons → proteinuria → intraglomerular HTN → capillary stretching
Proteinuria → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → capillary stretching → intraglomerular HTN
Intraglomerular HTN → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → proteinuria → capillary stretching
questions.exp: ↓ number of functional nephrons → hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons → intraglomerular hypertension → stretching of capillaries with ↑ pore diameter → proteinuria. (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: Stretching of glomerular capillaries in the CKD chain increases the capillary ______ diameter.
questions.exp: Stretching of capillaries → ↑ capillary pore diameter → proteinuria (albuminuria). (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: In the CKD chain, the interstitial-inflammation branch of proteinuria leads to formation of TGF-______.
questions.exp: Proteinuria splits into tubulotoxicity and interstitial inflammation; the inflammation branch gives TGF-β formation → tubulo interstitial fibrosis. (Book p730)

questions.q: The terminal step of the CKD pathophysiology flowchart after TGF-β formation is:
questions.exp: TGF-β formation → tubulo-interstitial fibrosis closes the chain. (Book p730)

questions.sec: Factors: passage through filtration barrier · p730
questions.q: By the size rule, effective diameter below which value (as printed) passes through the filtration barrier?
questions.exp: Size rule: effective diameter < 4 mm passes through. The scan prints 'mm' for every value on these size lines (nanometres are meant; the fenestration sizes on the same page correctly print 'nm') — taught as printed, flagged not corrected. (Book p730)

questions.q: By the size rule, substances with an effective diameter above which value do NOT pass the filtration barrier?
questions.exp: Size: effective diameter < 4 mm passes through; > 8–10 mm doesn't pass. The scan prints 'mm' for every value on these size lines (nanometres are meant; the fenestration sizes on the same page correctly print 'nm') — taught as printed, flagged not corrected. (Book p730)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the charge rule of the filtration barrier is TRUE?
opts: Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if they carry a negative charge
Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if positively charged
Charge plays no role between 4 and 8 mm
Only molecules above 10 mm are charge-repelled
questions.exp: Charge: effective diameter 4–8 mm is repelled if −ve charge (the 'repelled' note sits above the arrow). The scan prints 'mm' for every value on these size lines (nanometres are meant; the fenestration sizes on the same page correctly print 'nm') — taught as printed, flagged not corrected. (Book p730)

questions.q: The book's charge-rule example, albumin, has an effective diameter of:
questions.exp: Eg: albumin 7.6 mm, -vely charged — hence repelled despite sitting in the 4-8 mm window. The scan prints 'mm' for every value on these size lines (nanometres are meant; the fenestration sizes on the same page correctly print 'nm') — taught as printed, flagged not corrected. (Book p730)

questions.q: Match each label in the glomerular-capillary figure with the structure it marks — 1) Glomerular basement membrane 2) Podocyte 3) Foot processes … A) Membrane beneath the tuft cells  B) Projections hugging the capillary  C) Cell body whose label prints with a stray '7'
questions.exp: Glomerular basement membrane → the membrane beneath the tuft; podocyte → its cell body (the printed label reads 'Podocyte 7' — a stray '7' glyph sits just before the leader line); foot processes → the projections hugging the capillary. (Book p730)

questions.q: Match each label in the glomerular-capillary figure with the structure it marks — 1) Capillary 2) Capillary endothelium 3) Mesangial angle … A) The lumen seen in cross-section  B) Corner between capillary and mesangium  C) Lining of the capillary lumen
questions.exp: Capillary → the lumen in cross-section; capillary endothelium → its cellular lining; mesangial angle → the corner between capillary and mesangium. (Book p730)

questions.q: Match each label in the glomerular-capillary figure with the structure it marks — 1) Microfilaments 2) Mesangium 3) Mesangial matrix … A) Matrix material at the tuft base  B) The mesangial region proper  C) Cytoskeletal elements labelled inside the mesangial region
questions.exp: Microfilaments → cytoskeletal elements inside the mesangial region; mesangium → the mesangial region proper; mesangial matrix → the matrix at the tuft base. (Book p730)

questions.q: The glomerular cross-section figure on this page carries the caption:
questions.exp: Caption as printed: 'Glomerular capillary'. (Book p730)

questions.q: All of the following are labelled in the glomerular-capillary figure EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Figure labels: podocyte (printed with a stray '7'), glomerular basement membrane, foot processes, capillary, mesangial angle, capillary endothelium, microfilaments, mesangium and mesangial matrix; no slit diaphragm (that is diagrammed later with podocytes). (Book p730)

questions.q: The major constituent of the glomerular basement membrane is:
questions.exp: GBM constituent: type 4 collagen (majorly). (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each type-4 collagen configuration with its basement membrane — 1) α1 α1 α2 2) α3 α4 α5 3) α5 α5 α6 … A) Epidermal BM  B) GBM, cochlear BM and ocular BM  C) Present at birth
questions.exp: α1α1α2 at birth; α3α4α5 in GBM, cochlear BM and ocular BM; α5α5α6 in epidermal BM. (Book p731)

questions.q: A defect in type 4 collagen produces:
questions.exp: Type 4 collagen defect → Alport syndrome. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each Alport syndrome form with its profile — 1) The 85% form 2) The 10–15% form … A) AD/AR inheritance, α3+/α4 defect, normal skin stain B) X-linked inheritance, α5 defect, absent skin stain
opts: Both are X-linked with absent stain
Both are AD/AR with normal stain
questions.exp: 85% X-linked with alpha5 defect and absent skin/epidermal stain; 10-15% AD/AR with the printed 'alpha3+/ alpha4' defect cell and normal stain. The column header prints 'Immunoflorescence' (one u) — taught as printed. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: The negative charge of the GBM comes from heparin sulfate proteoglycans such as perlecan and ______.
questions.exp: Negative charge: heparin sulfate proteoglycans (eg: perlecan, agrin) — 'Heparin sulfate' is the printed spelling; standard nomenclature is heparan sulfate. (Book p731)

questions.q: In the GBM visualisation tree, the method listed first (printed as '1.') is:
questions.exp: Visualisation of GBM: 1. Electron m/s (microscope), paired with what is printed as 'a. Stains under light m/s' — the mixed '1.'/'a.' numbering is a source oddity, flagged not corrected. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: Under the light microscope the GBM is best seen with Gomori methenamine silver stain, preferred over Masson's ______.
questions.exp: Stains under light m/s (printed 'a.'): Gomori methenamine Silver Stain > masson's Trichrome ('masson's' lowercase is the printed form). (Book p731)

questions.q: Normal GBM thickness on electron microscopy is:
questions.exp: Thickness: normal 350–400 nm; thin GBM disease < 200 nm. (Book p731)

questions.q: Thin GBM disease is defined by a GBM thickness of:
questions.exp: Thin GBM disease: < 200 nm against a normal 350–400 nm. (Book p731)

questions.q: All of the following are true of the GBM EXCEPT:
opts: Its negative charge comes from podocalyxin
Its major constituent is type 4 collagen
It can be visualised by electron microscopy
questions.exp: GBM negative charge = heparin sulfate proteoglycans (perlecan, agrin); podocalyxin coats the endothelial fenestrations and podocyte slits. (Book p731)

questions.q: The supporting cells of the filtration barrier named in the book's note are the:
questions.exp: Note: supporting cells of the filtration barrier = mesangial cells. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: The constituent of mesangial cells listed in the note is ______.
questions.exp: Mesangial cell constituent: microfilaments. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: Violent contraction of mesangial cells ruptures the capillary and causes ______.
questions.exp: Violent contraction → rupture of capillary → macrohematuria; it also ↓ surface area → ↓ GFR. (Book p731)

questions.q: Mesangial contraction reduces the capillary surface area and therefore:
questions.exp: ↓ surface area → ↓ GFR. (Book p731)

questions.q: Mesangial proliferative disease is defined by more than how many mesangial cells in a space?
questions.exp: Mesangial cell/mesangial proliferative = >3 mesangial cells in a space. (Book p731)

questions.q: The m/c prototype disease of mesangial cell/matrix expansion listed is:
questions.exp: Mesangial cell expansion (matrix expansion)/glomerular disease: IgA nephropathy (m/c) prototype disease. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: In the light-microscope image legend, PT = proximal tubule and CL = ______.
questions.exp: Legend as printed: 'CL = capillary lumen' and 'PT = proximal tubule'; the photo also labels PT and CL directly. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each label in the light-microscope image with what its arrows mark — 1) Mesangial cells 2) Bowman's space 3) PT … A) Proximal tubule profiles  B) The urinary space around the tuft  C) Cells in the mesangial regions
questions.exp: Mesangial cells → cells in the mesangial regions; Bowman's space → the urinary space around the tuft; PT → proximal tubule profiles (legend: PT = proximal tubule). (Book p731)

questions.q: Match the remaining light-microscope image labels — 1) Open capillary loops 2) CL (four labels) … A) Abbreviation for capillary lumen used on the lumens B) Arrows marking the patent capillary profiles
opts: Both are parts of Bowman's capsule
questions.exp: Open capillary loops → arrows onto the patent capillary profiles; CL → the lumen abbreviation printed on those spaces (capillary lumen). (Book p731)

questions.q: All of the following are labelled in the light-microscope image EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Light microscope image labels mesangial cells, Bowman's space, PT (proximal tubule), CL (capillary lumen) and open capillary loops; the macula densa appears in the JGA figure. (Book p731)

questions.q: The left-hand figure on this page (the histology photograph) is captioned:
questions.exp: Caption as printed: 'Light microscope image'. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each label in the juxtaglomerular-apparatus figure with the structure it names — 1) PCT 2) GC 3) AA … A) Proximal convoluted tubule  B) Afferent arteriole  C) The four capillary circles inside the tuft
questions.exp: JGA figure abbreviations: PCT = proximal convoluted tubule; GC = the four glomerular capillary circles inside the tuft; AA = afferent arteriole. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each label in the juxtaglomerular-apparatus figure with the structure it names — 1) Parietal layer 2) DCT 3) Visceral layer … A) Distal convoluted tubule  B) Podocyte layer of the capsule  C) Outer layer of Bowman's capsule
questions.exp: Parietal layer → outer layer of Bowman's capsule; DCT → distal convoluted tubule; visceral layer → podocyte layer of the capsule. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match the remaining juxtaglomerular-apparatus labels — 1) EA 2) Macula densa … A) The plaque facing the glomerular tuft B) Efferent arteriole
opts: Both are part of the proximal tubule
questions.exp: EA = efferent arteriole; the macula densa plaque faces the glomerular tuft at the vascular pole. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each juxtaglomerular-apparatus figure label with its synonym — 1) JG cells 2) Lacis cells … A) Extraglomerular mesangial cells B) Granular cells
questions.exp: Figure: JG cells (granular cells); lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells), with macula densa, AA, EA, PCT, DCT, parietal and visceral layers. (Book p731)

questions.q: The right-hand figure on this page is captioned:
questions.exp: Caption as printed: 'Juxtaglomerular apparatus'. (Book p731)

questions.q: The slit diaphragm / filtration slits are defined as the space between:
questions.exp: Slit diaphragm/filtration slits: space btw 2 podocytes (the digit is a script '2', confirmed at 16x zoom; background OCR misread it as 'a'). (Book p732)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about podocytes is TRUE?
opts: They are terminally differentiated and cannot be regenerated
They are the main filtration site of the GBM
They lie inside the capillary lumen
questions.exp: Podocytes: terminally differentiated cells (cannot be regenerated). (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: Podocytes are anchored to the GBM by their ______, where no filtration occurs.
questions.exp: Anchored to GBM by foot processes: no filtration at the anchor. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each podocyte protein compartment with its proteins — 1) Inside 2) Surface … A) Podocin and TRPC6 B) α actinin 4
questions.exp: Proteins: inside = 'alpha actin 4' exactly as printed (standard nomenclature is alpha-actinin-4; flagged, not silently corrected); surface = podocin and TRPC6. (Book p732)

questions.q: The diameter given for the podocyte filtration slits (coated with podocalyxin) is:
questions.exp: Diameter: 30–50 nm, coated with podocalyxin (endothelial fenestrations are 50–100 nm). (Book p732)

questions.q: The function of the slit diaphragm / filtration slits is given as:
questions.exp: Function: filtration (preventing protein leak is the separately listed role of nephrins; anchoring is the job of podocyte foot processes). (Book p732)

questions.q: All of the following are true of nephrins EXCEPT:
opts: They are the angiotensin II binding receptors of podocytes
They are proteins contained in the slit diaphragm
questions.exp: Nephrins: proteins in the slit diaphragm, prevent protein leak, maintain podocyte integrity; angiotensin binds a separate angiotensin II binding receptor on the podocyte. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each label in figure (a) with what its leader marks — 1) Macula densa 2) Distal convoluted tubule 3) Afferent arteriole … A) Tubule section drawn beside the plaque at the top  B) Specialized plaque at the vascular pole  C) Vessel entering the tuft at the vascular pole
questions.exp: Macula densa → the specialized plaque at the vascular pole; distal convoluted tubule → the tubule section drawn beside it; afferent arteriole → the vessel entering the tuft. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each label in figure (a) with what its leader marks — 1) Efferent arteriole 2) Bowman's capsule 3) Mesangium … A) Vessel leaving the tuft  B) Central tissue between capillary loops  C) Cup surrounding the tuft
questions.exp: Efferent arteriole → the vessel leaving the tuft; Bowman's capsule → the cup surrounding the tuft; mesangium → the central tissue between capillary loops. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each label in figure (a) with what its leader marks — 1) Podocyte 2) Capillary 3) Fenestrated endothelium … A) Cells draped over the capillaries  B) Inner lining of the capillary profile  C) The capillary profiles inside the tuft
questions.exp: Podocyte → the cells draped over the capillaries; capillary → the capillary profiles inside the tuft; fenestrated endothelium → the inner lining of each profile. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match the remaining labels in figure (a) — 1) Glomerular basement membrane 2) Proximal tubule (labelled twice) … A) Tubule drawn at the bottom, labelled on both sides B) Membrane beneath the podocyte and endothelium
opts: Both label the same capillary wall layer
questions.exp: Glomerular basement membrane → the membrane beneath the podocyte/endothelium; proximal tubule → the tubule drawn at the bottom (the label is printed twice, on both sides). (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each label in figure (b) with what it marks — 1) F-actin 2) Slit diaphragm 3) Podocyte foot process … A) Cytoskeletal core inside the foot process  B) The bridge spanning the filtration slit  C) The two foot processes facing across the slit
questions.exp: F-actin → the cytoskeletal core inside the foot process; slit diaphragm → the bridge spanning the filtration slit; podocyte foot process → the pair of processes facing across it. (Book p732)

questions.q: In figure (b), the transmembrane proteoglycan pair labelled with beta and alpha subunits at the foot-process base is:
questions.exp: Figure (b) labels 'beta / alpha dystro-glycan' at both foot-process bases (the agrin labels below read 'Agrin' on the left but print 'Argin' on the right — a figure misspelling, flagged not corrected). (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: In the slit-diaphragm podocyte figure, α3β1 integrin anchors the foot process to the GBM via laminin-______.
questions.exp: Figure (b): alpha3beta1 integrin with Laminin-11 links the podocyte foot process to the glomerular basement membrane. 'Laminin-11' is the printed figure label (standard laminin nomenclature uses names like laminin-521/111) — taught as printed. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match the remaining labels in figure (b) — 1) 'Argin' (right label) 2) GEC 3) Glomerular basement membrane … A) The membrane on which the foot processes rest  B) The heparan-sulfate proteoglycan printed with a misspelled name  C) The endothelial cells drawn at the diagram base
questions.exp: 'Argin' (right; the left label spells 'Agrin') → the agrin proteoglycan of the GBM; GEC → the glomerular endothelial cells drawn at the base; glomerular basement membrane → the membrane on which the foot processes rest (labelled at the diagram base). (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each group of slit-diaphragm legend proteins with its legend column — 1) Nephrin, NEPH1, CD2AP, ZO-1, Podocin 2) Fat-1, NCK, ACTN4, ILK 3) CD151, TRPC6, Podocalyxin, Synaptopodin … A) Column 1  B) Column 2  C) Column 3
questions.exp: Legend reads column by column: column 1 = nephrin, NEPH1, CD2AP, ZO-1, podocin; column 2 = Fat-1, NCK, ACTN4, ILK; column 3 = CD151, TRPC6, podocalyxin, synaptopodin (names as printed). (Book p732)

questions.q: All of the following appear in the figure's protein legend EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Laminin-11 is a diagram label, not a legend entry; synaptopodin, ACTN4 and podocalyxin are legend entries. (Book p732)

questions.q: The two panels on this page share the single caption:
questions.exp: Shared caption as printed: 'Slit diaphragm podocytes'. (Book p732)

questions.q: Angiotensin binding to the podocyte's angiotensin II binding receptor causes:
questions.exp: Angiotensin binds podocyte angiotensin II binding receptor → downregulation of nephrin. (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: Loss of podocyte integrity in this chain is termed ______.
questions.exp: Downregulation of nephrin → loss of podocyte integrity (podocytopathies). (Book p732)

questions.q: A patient with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is found to have podocytes in the urine. In the book's angiotensin-podocyte chain, podocyturia is the stage immediately after:
questions.exp: Chain: loss of podocyte integrity (podocytopathies) → podocyte detached → podocyturia → podocytopenia → GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells. (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: After podocytopenia the GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells, producing ______ formation.
questions.exp: GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells → synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis. (Book p732)

questions.q: The last two steps of the podocyte-loss chain before CKD are synechiae formation followed by:
questions.exp: Synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis → CKD. (Book p732)

questions.q: Which sequence matches the book's podocyte-loss chain?
opts: Podocyte detached → podocyturia → podocytopenia → GBM attaches to parietal cells → synechiae → glomerulosclerosis → CKD
Podocyturia → podocyte detached → podocytopenia → synechiae → CKD
questions.exp: Full chain: angiotensin binds the podocyte angiotensin II binding receptor → downregulation of nephrin → loss of podocyte integrity (podocytopathies) → podocyte detached → podocyturia → podocytopenia → GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells → synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis → CKD. (Book p732)

questions.q: ARBs/ACE inhibitors are used in the Rx of diabetic nephropathy in order to:
opts: Block the angiotensin II receptor on podocytes
questions.exp: ARBs /ACEI(-)'s used in Rx of diabetic nephropathy to block Angiotensin II Receptor, as printed. Source simplification flagged: ARBs block the angiotensin II receptor while ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation. (Book p732)

questions.q: In congenital nephrotic syndrome, DMS stands for:
questions.exp: Congenital nephrotic syndrome: DMS = diffuse mesangial Sclerosis (capital S printed mid-line). (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each cell of the Finnish-type nephrotic-syndrome row — 1) Inheritance 2) Defect 3) Age … A) AR  B) Birth  C) Nephrin : NPHS1
questions.exp: Finnish-type row: inheritance AR; defect nephrin (printed 'Nephrin : NPHS1' with a subscript 1); age — birth. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: The outcome of Finnish type nephrotic syndrome is 100% ______.
questions.exp: Finnish type: outcome 100% mortality, histology ≡ DMS, management dash. (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Finnish-type row is TRUE?
opts: Histology ≡ DMS with the management cell a dash
Histology ≡ FSGS with renal transplant listed
questions.exp: Finnish-type row: histology ≡ DMS (printed with the equivalence sign) and the management cell is a bare dash (nothing listed). (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each cell of the podocin-type row — 1) Inheritance 2) Defect 3) Age … A) AR  B) 3-5 years  C) Podocin
questions.exp: Podocin-type row: inheritance AR; defect podocin; age — 3-5 years. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: The outcome of the podocin type is 100% steroid resistance progressing to ______.
questions.exp: Podocin-type outcome cell: '100% Steroid resistance → CKD'. (Book p733)

questions.q: A 4-year-old has nephrotic syndrome with 100% steroid resistance and FSGS-equivalent histology. The table's listed management is:
questions.exp: Podocin-type row: histology ≡ FSGS, management = renal transplant (the autosomal dominant type repeats these cells). (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each cell of the autosomal dominant-type row — 1) Inheritance 2) Defect 3) Age … A) alpha actinin 4/TRPC6  B) AD  C) Adolescence
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant-type row: inheritance AD; defect 'alpha actinin 4/TRPC6' as printed (TRPC6 with a subscript 6); age — adolescence. (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the autosomal dominant-type row is TRUE?
opts: Its outcome, histology and management match the podocin type
questions.exp: The AD-type outcome/histology/management cells repeat the podocin-type cells: 100% steroid resistance → CKD, ≡ FSGS, renal transplant. (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each congenital nephrotic syndrome type with its defect and age — 1) Finnish type 2) Podocin type 3) Autosomal dominant type … A) Podocin defect at 3–5 years  B) Nephrin (NPHS1) defect at birth  C) α actinin 4/TRPC6 defect at adolescence
questions.exp: Finnish type: AR, nephrin NPHS1, birth; podocin type: AR, podocin, 3–5 years; AD type: α actinin 4/TRPC6, adolescence. (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the congenital nephrotic syndrome table is TRUE?
opts: The Finnish type is the only type with 100% mortality
All three types are inherited as AR
The podocin type presents at birth
The autosomal dominant type has histology ≡ DMS
questions.exp: Only the Finnish-type row lists 100% mortality; the AD type is AD (not AR); the podocin type presents at 3-5 years; the AD type is ≡ FSGS. (Book p733)

questions.q: Finnish type nephrotic syndrome is m/c seen in:
opts: Premature babies with a large placenta
questions.exp: Finnish type nephrotic syndrome m/c seen in premature babies with large placenta. (Book p733)

questions.q: Besides congenital nephrotic syndrome, DMS is also seen in:
questions.exp: Note as printed: DMS also seen in 'Denys Drash Syndrome' (no hyphen in the print). (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each filtration-barrier site with its disease — 1) Endothelium 2) GBM 3) Mesangium … A) Alport  B) IgA nephropathy  C) PSGN
questions.exp: Site–disease: endothelium = PSGN; GBM = Alport; mesangium = IgA nephropathy. (Book p733)

questions.q: All of the following sit under 'podocyte with podocytopenia' EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Podocyte with podocytopenia: diabetes, FSGS, membranous; MCD sits under podocyte without podocytopenia. (Book p733)

questions.q: The disease listed under 'podocyte without podocytopenia' is:
questions.exp: Without podocytopenia: mCD (printed with a lowercase m). (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following site–disease pairings is TRUE as written in the book?
questions.exp: The table pairs GBM with Alport, endothelium with PSGN and mesangium with IgA nephropathy. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: In the site–disease table, the endothelial site corresponds to the disease ______.
questions.exp: Endothelium → PSGN in the site–disease table. (Book p733)
